author: high
claim: Every maximum-length trail T in G is closed.
evidence: Write T as v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_k,v_k. Such a trail exists because G is finite and has at least one edge. Suppose v_0 and v_k are distinct. Counting incidences at v_k among the edges of T, each arrival before the final arrival is paired with a later departure, while the final arrival is unpaired; hence T uses an odd number of incidences at v_k. The total degree of v_k is even, so at least one edge incident with v_k is not used by T. Appending that edge produces a longer trail, contradicting the choice of T. Thus v_0=v_k.

links.statement: Every maximum-length trail T in G is closed.

glossary.G: the finite connected undirected graph in the problem
glossary.T: a trail of maximum possible number of edges in G
glossary.V(T): the set of vertices occurring on T

author: high
claim: A maximum-length closed trail T in the connected graph G traverses every edge.
evidence: Assume an edge f is not used by T and choose an endpoint x of f. If x lies on T, then f itself is an unused edge incident with V(T). Otherwise, connectedness supplies a path from x to V(T); choose one of minimum length and let g be its last edge, whose endpoint w lies in V(T). The other endpoint of g does not lie in V(T), by minimality, so g cannot be an edge of T. Thus in all cases an unused edge g is incident with some w in V(T). Since T is closed, cyclically rotate its edge-vertex sequence to make w its initial and terminal vertex, then append g. This is a trail longer than T, a contradiction.

links.statement: A maximum-length closed trail T in the connected graph G traverses every edge.
